transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-01-13
Start time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen, Ravi Patel, Sofia Alvarez (Redwood) — Eleanor Park, Jonas Meyer, Priya Nair, Sam Ortiz (Verdant)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro we are Maya AE, Ravi is our solutions eng who will run the bench plan with you. Sofia is on for notes. Eleanor, do you want to kick off with the high level goals?

[00:18] Eleanor Park: Sure yeah thanks Maya. At Verdant we're building an assistant that ingests sensor telemetry and regulatory filings and produces compliance summaries and incident narratives. Main goals for the POC are: 1) show latency and cost at ~2k tokens per interaction, 2) extraction accuracy on our domain entities above 92% for high-priority fields, 3) bilingual support — English and Spanish first, French later. Timeline ideally four weeks to pilot, then expand.

[00:50] Jonas Meyer: And just to add, product needs deterministic summarization for regs — can't hallucinate stuff; we need high precision and traceable sources. Also we want to compare open weights because of license flexibility.

[01:05] Ravi Patel: Got it. Quick qualification, what's your current throughput expectation? steady at around 4 rps during business hours, spike to maybe 12 rps? and typical context window — do you expect 2k tokens as a single request or multi-turn?

[01:25] Eleanor Park: Typical single request ~1.5k tokens including context and a few attachments; bursts maybe 10-15 concurrent. Not huge, but latency matters for UX.

[01:40] Priya Nair: On infra, we can't send PII to hosted endpoints in prod due to contracts. For the POC we can blur or synth the data, but we do want to test private deployment (VPC) and peering. Security/compliance is a blocker.

[02:05] Maya Chen: Totally — Redwood supports private deployment and VPC peering. For the POC we can do a hybrid: run bench on Redwood hosted endpoints with redacted data, and then a small private node for network/perf validation. We'll share SOC2 docs.

[02:22] Sam Ortiz: We'll need KMS integration and audit logs for any private run. Also retention rules — data must be wiped after 30 days.

[02:38] Sofia Alvarez: Noted, we'll include KMS/HSM options and audit log config in the security pack.

[02:45] Jonas Meyer: Back to models — what are you proposing for shortlist? we want open-source models that balance quality vs cost; multilingual is important.

[03:00] Ravi Patel: Based on your needs I suggest a three-tier shortlist: 1) high-quality multi-lingual: Mistral polyglot variant (we'll test a 34B-ish), 2) balanced cost/quality: Llama 2 13B / a SFTed variant, 3) lightweight low-cost: quantized 7B family (we can test Mistral 7B or LlaMA-7b Q4). We'll also include a Redwood-verified medium model for a baseline (call it 'redwood-bench-compat' in the plan).

[03:35] Eleanor Park: Are there known gaps for regulatory language? legalese tends to trip up many open models.

[03:45] Ravi Patel: Right. For legal/regulatory summarization we need models with good long-context behavior and fact-grounding. We'll evaluate on two axes: generative fidelity (does the summary introduce false facts) and extraction accuracy (field-level recall/precision). For generative fidelity we'll use a hallucination score derived from human labels and an automatic citation alignment metric.

[04:10] Maya Chen: Also to be realistic, quantized 7B models will be cheaper but might struggle with the nuance. We should set acceptance thresholds per model class, e.g., 92% extraction for high-tier, 88% for mid-tier, 80% for low-tier — those are examples for discussion.

[04:40] Jonas Meyer: That helps. What's the proposed bench setup and what metrics will you return?

[04:50] Ravi Patel: We'll measure: median and p95 latency (cold vs warm), tokens per second, cost per 1k tokens (estimate based on hosting + infra), extraction precision/recall/F1 on labeled set, summarization fact error rate, and a multilingual consistency metric (compare EN-ES outputs on mirrored prompts). We'll provide raw model outputs, diff annotations, and a scoring sheet.

[05:20] Eleanor Park: For multilingual tests, we can provide paired EN/ES samples — sometimes translations change the meaning, we want parity.

[05:28] Priya Nair: On throughput, you mentioned continuous batching and KV cache earlier in docs; what's the expected latency penalty for batching? because our UI needs under 800ms p50 ideally.

[05:42] Ravi Patel: Batching improves throughput but increases tail latency. For small QPS like yours, continuous batching with micro-batches will keep p50 close to single-request latency. We'll include both single-request and batched runs. KV cache helps for multi-turn chat contexts but adds memory overhead; we'll test enabling/disabling cache for representative flows.

[06:10] Maya Chen: timeline proposal: week 0 (this week) finalize scope and test data; week 1 run initial bench across the 3 model tiers with small sample; week 2 full graph run with multilingual and larger set; week 3 private infra perf and an in-depth QA pass; week 4 wrap-up, review, and recommendation. Does that align?

[06:34] Eleanor Park: Yes that fits internal planning. We'll need a final decision point at the end of week 4 to move to pilot.

[06:45] Jonas Meyer: One question on cost modeling: can you provide token-cost estimates for each model under typical workload assumptions?

[06:55] Ravi Patel: Yes we'll include cost-per-100k tokens under hosted and dedicated assumptions, and an extrapolated monthly spend for the expected throughput. We'll show sensitivity to batch size and quantization.

[07:10] Sam Ortiz: Security again: during the private node run we need to confirm RBAC mapping to our IdP and that audit logs have per-request metadata including user id and prompt hash.

[07:24] Sofia Alvarez: We'll surface RBAC and SAML SSO integration notes and confirm that audit logs include the fields you asked for.

[07:32] Eleanor Park: On evaluation: what's the human labeling effort we need to commit? We have a small internal compliance team but not large labeling resources.

[07:45] Ravi Patel: For high-quality evals we recommend a 200-400 sample human-labeled set for extraction and another 100-200 for summarization ground truth. If that's too heavy we can do a smaller core set and use automated heuristics for coverage. Redwood can help with a labeling template but we don't provide full labeling services by default.

[08:10] Jonas Meyer: We'll try to prioritize 250 extraction samples across EN/ES and 120 summarization checks.

[08:22] Maya Chen: Great — let's talk about acceptance criteria more concretely. Eleanor, does Verdant prioritize extraction precision over recall?

[08:31] Eleanor Park: Precision is more important; false positives in a regulatory report are costly. So our success criteria: extraction precision >= 92% for core fields, summarization hallucination < 2% on the labeled set, p50 latency < 700ms on private node, and token-cost below our threshold TBD (we'll give you a target).

[09:00] Ravi Patel: We'll map those to pass/fail gates in the bench. For example if the mid-tier model meets those gates we can recommend it; otherwise we recommend canarying the higher-tier model.

[09:14] Priya Nair: For private node testing, we need network diagrams and a simple terraform snippet to provision the test VM. Can Redwood provide a quickstart?

[09:26] Maya Chen: Yes, we have a private deployment quickstart and a terraform module. We'll share it in the security pack.

[09:33] Jonas Meyer: One wild card — we might test a domain-adapted checkpoint. Is there an easy path to SFT or LoRA fine-tuning in the POC?

[09:44] Ravi Patel: For a 4-week sprint, we can include a small LoRA experiment on the mid-tier model if you can provide 5k-10k in-domain examples; training time depends on instance sizes. We'll keep it as an optional stretch goal and show delta in extraction accuracy.

[10:02] Eleanor Park: We can assemble a small seed dataset if that helps.

[10:07] Sofia Alvarez: Noted as optional LoRA trial.

[10:12] Maya Chen: Any competitor or procurement constraints from your side?

[10:18] Sam Ortiz: We prefer open models due to license clarity and avoid vendor lock. Procurement also wants a clear exit plan and data deletion guarantees.

[10:28] Maya Chen: Understood. Redwood's private option gives you that control. We'll include exit procedure docs.

[10:35] Jonas Meyer: For the bench deliverable, what's the format? spreadsheet, pdf, raw outputs?

[10:42] Ravi Patel: A spreadsheet with scores, a short slide deck with key recommendations, and a tarball of raw model outputs and annotations. We'll also give a reproducible script to replay the bench locally.

[10:55] Eleanor Park: Good — that helps us with procurement.

[11:02] Maya Chen: Alright let's recap next steps: Redwood sends bench template + security pack by Friday 1/16, Verdant provides sample datasets and acceptance targets by 1/18, Priya will spin up a test VPC node by 1/19, bench initial run week of 1/20. Owners and dates in action items. Anything else?

[11:20] Jonas Meyer: Please include a small example prompt set that simulates noisy sensor text and truncated attachments — that's a common failure mode.

[11:30] Ravi Patel: We'll include noise-robust prompt variants and file-attachment heuristics.

[11:36] Sam Ortiz: Also please include proof that audit logs are immutable and the schema.

[11:42] Maya Chen: We'll include audit log schema in the security docs.

[11:48] Eleanor Park: Sounds good. we're aligned. Thanks everyone.

[11:52] Maya Chen: Thanks all — we'll follow up with the pack and schedule infra call.

End of meeting.

Notes on transcript quality: speaker overlaps and names occasionally mis-attributed by auto transcript; some technical terms transcribed as similar-sounding words (e.g., 'K-V cache' vs 'KV cache', 'LoRA' occasionally capitalized differently).
